comments.author: @JohnSmith762A11B
comments.text: Every school I've ever attended taught me at perhaps 3 percent of my learning capacity. Classic schooling is a sort of deathtrap for most kids. Schools don't educate: they regiment. Compulsory schooling arose to prepare children for factory work, and that is still the model today even though most factory work is gone. We don't need AI augmenting and assisting traditional classrooms, we need school displaced entirely by highly and individually optimised teaching and tutoring systems that can have children educated to college level by around age 13. What is needed are systems that can spend time speaking with and learning to understand how a particular child learns best and then teach and tutor a child in that exact style, using metaphors that particular child grasps readily. As far as socialisation, that should happen in environments outside of school such as community play and sporting events and shared cultural activities. Enough of this failed traditional thinking that is producing hordes of barely educated and unhappy young people.

comments.author: @lunaticfringe23
comments.text:
As a teacher, I have to agree with the commentary about the origins and current state of public education. You're right about where it came from and who it was designed to serve. At its core, it’s meant to provide a baseline education up to a certain point, with parental involvement as a supplement. But over the years, this dynamic has shifted significantly. Nowadays, especially in the post-COVID era, teachers have been reduced to glorified babysitters in many people's eyes.

Education desperately needs a change. A foundational pedagogy model, or perhaps an agentic system for building curriculum, could be a good start. Imagine a system with specialized agents handling different aspects of education: one to research subjects based on provided standards, another to build a curriculum framework and flesh out student objectives, and finally, a model to deliver and pace material based on real-time formative assessments. This could even take into account factors like student engagement through body language, tone of voice, or interaction responses.

For decades, we've been pushing the entire profession uphill, trying to serve a post-modern student while blaming teachers when even the best, research-backed strategies can’t compete with the allure of TikTok or Fortnite. Add to that the ongoing effort by certain political factions to undermine public education, funneling public money into private business ventures. Sadly, it’s likely that true innovation will come from these efforts to privatize education, as public ed faces increasing challenges.

The key, though, is watching the gap between high-level pedagogy theories and what actually works in classrooms. Most teachers will tell you that the "ivory tower" ideas don’t hold up in practice. So, if we’re going to build a new model, we need to focus on the insights and strategies from teachers who are actually in the trenches. Because right now, most foundational AI models only half work in a real classroom setting.

Great video but you have it backwards about "scaling loss".  1:30 --  You said "the more compute we throw at it, the better it gets.".  In fact scaling loss is the opposite and is a negative thing.  From ChatGPT itself:

"In the context of AI, scaling loss refers to the phenomenon where the performance gains of an AI model do not increase proportionally with the increase in model size or the amount of training data. As models get larger, their performance on tasks such as accuracy, generalization, or loss function improvement can plateau or even deteriorate."

comments.author: @roguevariables
comments.text:
There is already an enormous "semi-synthetic" corpus for use by AI: the conversation records.

AI companies are sitting on the goldmine that it needs for the next step. With 200 million weekly users on OpenAI alone, these conversations capture real-world interactions, problem-solving, and dynamic thought processes that are far richer than static datasets. The back-and-forth nature of conversations could accelerate AI’s ability to handle nuanced, multi-turn dialogues and better model human cognition.

Obviously, privacy is important, but with proper anonymization and opt-in options, a lot of users would likely be open to contributing their data for AI training if they saw the value as I do. These conversations offer diverse, real-time feedback that could significantly advance AI's ability to think and reason like a human.

This is an early variant of AI learning from itself, by studying interactions between itself and humans. The first start? Give people a way to "donate" their chat record to the effort, with an appropriate release acceptance.
